Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers.
  • The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

Industry observers note that for example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

In a recent development, more Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats.

It has been revealed that perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will promptly soak up water.

According to recent reports, these Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no problems.

Industry observers note that they use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a massive fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Industry observers note that near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

Industry observers note that these gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold swiftly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

Sources indicate that these pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

In a recent development, I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to promptly type out a text message on an iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

The gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

The secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Sources indicate that bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

Several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too major, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

It has been revealed that an easy way to spot a glove that’s too major is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying fresh gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

In a recent development, if you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

Most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

Recent findings suggest that for the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can promptly turn into frozen prunes.

It has been revealed that gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

It has been revealed that regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very important in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

It has been revealed that the palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

According to recent reports, if you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

'I Ran 3 Miles A Day For 21 Days—Here's What I Learned About My Brain And Body'

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run.
  • I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

It has been revealed that but before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

By week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

There’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Industry observers note that whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

Sources indicate that I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty rapidly after starting or stopping a latest exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

Recent findings suggest that going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise shows that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

Industry observers note that around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

According to recent reports, before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

After a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

According to recent reports, it’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

The momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a new routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason upcoming runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”.

Want to try running three miles a day for yourself? These things made all the difference:.

It has been revealed that if your goal is to feel stronger, sleep better, and just feel a little more capable and confident—all with minimal equipment or cost—then yes, 100 percent. You don’t need a marathon medal to call yourself a runner or to be consistent. You just need a pair of sneakers, a bit of stick-to-it-ness, and a willingness to start where you are.

Sources indicate that and if you happen to find yourself romanticizing the idea of making a daily jog a habit? I say lean into it.

But this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

About the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

In a recent development, about the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

What we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

About the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

What we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

Industry observers note that about the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

What we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. Sadly, the one I checked out on the Significant Island was bonkers expensive and didn’t make sense for a gift, so I shopped around for something similar that wouldn’t break the bank. Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

Recent findings suggest that few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

In a recent development, what we gifted (and why): Jordan might spend more time in the saddle than any of us editors, and she knows her gear as well as anyone, especially what the pros are presently using. 10-Minute Slow Yoga Practice to Counter the Chaos

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that yoga isn’t the answer to everything.
  • The challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down.
  • Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that yoga isn’t the answer to everything. But when life gets stressful, your mat is a safe place to land. Amid moments of stress and chaos, a gentle yoga flow made up of intentional movement can help still your racing mind, regulate your breathing, and encourage overall well-being. This practice blends elements of yin yoga and a generally pared-down approach that feels like a truly restful beat rather than another item on your to-do list.

The challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down. It’s almost like you’re retraining your body, and reminding yourself that it’s okay to do so.

Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.

It has been revealed that begin in Rock Pose today, which is a variation of Child’s Pose. Sit back on your heels, with your toes untucked, and keep your legs close together. Hinge forward to round your upper body over your legs, placing your forehead on your mat or a block. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing upward, so you create a rock-like shape.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Industry observers note that extend your arms forward and press up onto your hands and knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

Recent findings suggest that lower yourself all the way down onto the front side of your body. Widen your feet toward the back corners of your mat. Your elbows will be just underneath your shoulders—or slightly forward if you’re dealing with lower back tension. Then lift your chest and press your palms and forearms into the mat in Sphinx Pose.

If you have a block, you can use it on its highest setting by angling it toward you and allowing your forehead to rest against the support.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Still lying down, stack your hands, elbows bent and pointing toward the edges of mat, and rest your forehead on the backs of your hands.

Start to slide your right knee out to the right side of the mat so it’s about in line with your hip in Half Frog. You want your right leg to have about a 90-degree angle so the inner thigh and calf are facing the floor. Keep resting your forehead on your hands or turn your head to one side.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

When you’re ready, repeat on the opposite side.

From Half Frog Pose with your left knee bent, take a deep breath in. As you exhale, let your left leg extend long and straight behind you. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing up. Turn your head and your gaze in either direction and let your shoulders round toward the ground. Simply be.

Stay here in a reverse variation of Savasana for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Sources indicate that tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

While I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

According to recent reports, the variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a latest lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

It has been revealed that the Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

In a recent development, senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also said, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”.

Sources indicate that on the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he said.

Garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

In a recent development, however, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

Sources indicate that jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He stated, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”.

Recent findings suggest that while the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

Recent findings suggest that if you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

Garmin’s new Forerunner 70 isn’t really an update of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

Recent findings suggest that the Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

Sources indicate that garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are currently testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

According to recent reports, at 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

While the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

Garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

In a recent development, as the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

According to recent reports, if you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

In a recent development, not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

In a recent development, mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

Recent findings suggest that triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

According to recent reports, the Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

The Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

The Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Recent findings suggest that finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#56719. A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (564 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral.
  • "Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.
  • The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and Fresh York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the Upcoming York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex.".

It has been revealed that her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified.".

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Recent findings suggest that sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing plans, Sager mentioned she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:.

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ.".

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#56718. These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4100 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking.
  • Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking. The air is crisp, the dirt is grippy, and we can’t wait to head to the singletrack after work and on weekends for great rides. And more than ever, like many other mountain bikers, we’re choosing E-MTBs for our rides. Electric mountain bikes help you maximize those rides and spend more time on your favorite trails.

Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail. And while heavier than traditional mountain bikes, these pedal-assist models allow you to cover more miles, ride faster, and tackle challenging climbs.

E-MTBs are engineered for performance on singletrack trails and deep in the woods. And while their low-power motors provide a boost when pedalling, E-MTBs are not electric motorcycles. You still have to pedal an electric mountain bike; you can’t simply twist a throttle and blast down the trail.

The best E-MTBs blend mountain bike components, suspension, and geometry with electronic technology in a brilliant fashion. Like non-electric mountain bikes, some E-MTBs blur the lines of XC and lightweight trail bikes, while others are burlier and take suspension and geometry cues from the top-performing enduro and downhill racing mountain bikes.

Sources indicate that aventon recently launched the Current, the brand’s first full-suspension E-MTB, and it is a gem! The Current ADV offers incredible value, and it’s trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, mentioned, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers. The Current’s motor and interface provide riders with a wide range of tuning options and lots of data.”.

Sources indicate that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor boasting 750 peak Watts and 110Nm torque. (The Current also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and torque to 120Nm.) Rounding out the ADV are a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

It has been revealed that in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab especially likes the Current’s intuitive and easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data and the ability to tune the motor settings.

Want a carbon frame and electronic drivetrain? The Current EXP is a great package for $5,999.

It has been revealed that specialized’s Turbo motor is a benchmark for electric mountain bike performance. It has plenty of power and torque, and the Morgan Hill, California-based brand has updated, polished, and refined the motor over several years. However, the biggest downside to Specialized E-MTBs has been their very steep starting price. But that has changed.

It has been revealed that specialized’s newest Levo model brings the platform to a more palatable $5,000 price. The Turbo Levo 4 Alloy uses the same motor and battery as the pricier carbon-chassis Expert model but with an aluminum frame, heavier components, and mechanical shifting to save pennies. The brand bolts its 105Nm torque and 810-watt Turbo 3.1 motor to a 150mm-travel, full-suspension aluminum frame and equips the bike with value-packed parts. SRAM brakes, a mechanical drivetrain, and Marzocchi suspension highlight the alloy Levo 4’s component package.

Hardtail mountain bikes are a gateway into the sport for many riders because they’re simple, sturdy, and affordable. Plus, big, burly full-suspension mountain bikes aren’t for everyone. For some riders, they’re overkill—adding cost and complexity without delivering benefits that match their needs. Hardtail E-MTBs provide pedal assistance for about the same price as full-suspension non-electric mountain bikes.

It has been revealed that when launched two years ago, the Ramblas impressed me with its great performance and capability for the price—and Aventon’s recent upgrades make it even better on the trail. The revised Ramblas ADV’s trail-forward components include a RockShox Psylo fork with 35mm stanchions, a 1x12 SRAM Eagle drivetrain that can handle most climbs, powerful four-piston SRAM DB6 brakes, and a useful dropper seatpost. The ADV’s tubeless rims and 2.4-inch Maxxis tires are also upgrades. These components are unmatched by any other hardtail E-MTB, especially at this price.

Superlight e-MTBs offer an intriguing compromise: In exchange for a less powerful drive unit, you get a lighter bike that feels and handles more like an analog mountain bike.

With the Turbo Levo R, Specialized asks: What if you didn’t need to compromise?

According to recent reports, the Levo R has the same drive unit and battery as the Levo 4, but in a lighter, shorter-travel package with matched 29-inch wheels. It’s around 5 pounds lighter than a standard Levo 4 at the same price. In the top-of-the-line S-Works trim, the DU offers up to 111 Nm of torque and 850 watts of peak power with an 850 or 900Wh battery. The 41.4-pound (18.8 kg) S-Works Ultralight uses a 600Wh battery to save weight. Lower-priced models offer 105 Nm, 810 watts, and an 840Wh battery.

It has been revealed that after spending the better part of a year riding an S-Works Levo R (46.7 lb., size S3), senior test editor Matt Phillips calls it a winning combination for many riders. “It has all the capability and range of a massive battery and full-power DU, but in a bike that’s much more flickable, lively, and, frankly, easier to ride than a heavier and bigger-travel e-MTB.” He says Specialized’s e-MTB hardware, frames, and suspension are the icing on top, and calls the Levo R one of the most entertaining mountain bikes, powered or unpowered, he’s ridden this year.

In a recent development, the 29-inch-wheeled Cannondale Moterra 4 has a subdued appearance, which makes it a sleeper. Many full-suspension E-MTBs routinely cost more than $10,000. However, Cannondale keeps the Moterra 4 to a more modest $5,500 while still packing a lot of punch for its price.

Sources indicate that at the heart of the Moterra is a trusty Bosch Performance Line CX motor mounted on a 150mm-travel aluminum full-suspension frame. And inside the bike’s stout downtube is a 600Wh Bosch battery. Cannondale’s product team made smart component choices—such as the excellent Shimano Cues drivetrain and 160mm-travel SR Suntour Xeron air-sprung fork—that save cost without sacrificing much performance. The Moterra 4 also has a long-travel dropper seatpost, tubeless wheels, and Tektro disc brakes.

If you buy the Moterra 4 through rei.com, you can have it shipped to your nearest REI location for professional assembly with in-store or curbside pickup. You also get one year of free adjustments—or two years if you’re an REI Co-op member.

According to recent reports, “I’ve never considered an e-bike a replacement for a traditional bike—until now.” That’s what Matt Phillips remarked in his review of the excellent S-Works Turbo Levo 4. The latest version of Specialized’s flagship e-MTB is refined, quiet, fun to ride, and refreshingly free of the common annoyances that plague many e-bikes.

Several standout features set the latest S-Works Turbo Levo 4 apart from the crowded E-MTB segment: a powerful motor delivering 111Nm of torque, a larger 900 Wh battery, and the ability to toggle the pedal-assist cutoff between Class 2 (20mph) and Class 3 (28mph). That extra speed might sound excessive, but it’s a welcome boost when you're riding to or between trails.

Though the S-Works Levo 4 is less expensive than its predecessor, it’s still eye-wateringly pricey at $12,500. For better value—relatively speaking—we recommend the Turbo Levo 4 Expert. It offers the same carbon frame, battery, and motor as the pricier model, though with slightly less torque. A 160mm-travel Fox 38 Performance Elite GRIPX2 fork and a Fox Float X Performance Elite shock handle suspension duties, and SRAM’s GX AXS drivetrain handles gear changes.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs, yet it’s packed with value. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Nm of torque) and a 430Wh battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, the Moraine has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

Sources indicate that the frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system used by Pivot), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain with four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the component selection on this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

According to recent reports, one advantage of an e-MTB is climbing faster and with less effort, leaving you fresher for the descent. A long-travel bike helps you make the most of that on steep, rough trails. It’s like having a personal chairlift for lapping downhill trails.

Recent findings suggest that cannondale’s Moterra Carbon LT 2 pairs a Bosch Performance Line CX motor and 750Wh battery with 165mm of plush, coil-sprung rear travel and a 170mm fork. Its frame combines a carbon front triangle with an alloy swingarm. Size-specific suspension kinematics tailor the suspension performance to each frame size. The mullet setup pairs a 29-inch front wheel with a 27.5-inch rear, giving you more room to move behind the saddle on steep terrain while keeping the larger front wheel’s rollover advantage. The battery is removable for off-bike charging.

For riders who prioritize steep descents and the refinement and reliability of a Bosch drive unit, the Moterra LT 2 is a strong choice.

It’s no exaggeration to say Avinox reshaped the performance e-MTB market. Developed and launched by drone maker DJI before becoming an independent organization, Avinox set new benchmarks with the M1: 105 Nm of torque and up to 1,000 watts of peak power. It also matched or exceeded established brands in features, function, and assist performance. Suddenly, longtime players were off the back, some way off the back.

Sources indicate that before they could catch up, Avinox followed the M1 with the more powerful, refined M2S: up to 150 Nm of torque and 1,500 watts of peak power. But power isn’t the whole story. Senior features director Louis Mazzante states the M2S “isn’t the thunderously loud, chassis-shaking hot-rod motor that its power suggests. It is quiet. It’s smooth. It’s refined.” He also praises its feature-packed, easy-to-use app and touch-screen controls, and says the motor’s power is smooth and tractable.

That blend of power, control, and features has made the M2S highly desirable to bike brands. Ari’s Wire Peak 3.0 stands out as an affordable way to get it.

In a recent development, starting at $4,999, the Wire Peak pairs the M2S with an 800Wh battery in an aluminum frame with 150mm of rear travel and a 160mm fork. This setup delivers up to 150 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,300 watts of peak power. The bike also has a four-bar suspension design, 29-inch or mullet wheel compatibility, and independent high/low and long/short geometry adjustments.

Sources indicate that ari delivers each bike directly to the buyer with a rider-specific setup. Buyers can customize the build through the configurator, and Ari will accommodate most off-menu parts and upgrade requests.

Recent findings suggest that after his first rides on his long-term test bike, senior test editor Matt Phillips called the chassis excellent, Ari’s buying process superb, and the drive unit best in class. He says the Wire Peak would be his choice if he were buying an e-MTB today.

The DRT 1.1 (from REI’s in-house Co-Op Cycles brand) is a good pick if you’re looking for an electric mountain bike to explore mellower trails and ride around town. REI equips the bikes with a dependable Bosch Performance Line mid-drive motor and internal battery.

It has been revealed that this hardtail rolls on tubeless-compatible 27.5-inch wheels with 2.6-inch-wide Maxxis Rekon tires for off-road capability. The DRT’s 100mm-travel SR Suntour fork with thru axle isn’t glamorous, but it works. The only notable component missing is a dropper seatpost; it would enhance the bike’s trail capability and help riders feel more confident on challenging terrain.

Traditional analog mountain bikes are usually grouped by frame travel. E-MTBs, on the other hand, are categorized by their power. However, more power ≠ more better. Pick the style that suits your riding needs, budget, and local trail access.

According to recent reports, ⚡️ Full-Power E-MTBs are the most common style and are generally equipped with roughly 750-watt peak power (1 horsepower) and 85 torque, or more. Bosch, Shimano, and Specialized are three commonly used motor brands for these bikes.

⚡️ Lightweight E-MTBs feature motors with less power and torque (50 to 60 Nm) and lower-capacity batteries. As a result, these bikes weigh less than other E-MTBs and ride more like an unassisted mountain bike, but with a little help on the climbs. Lightweight electric mountain bikes are less popular now than a couple of years ago, which means you can score good deals on great riding bikes.

⚡️ High-power e-MTBs are the newest category of electric mountain bikes, and they’re quickly becoming one of the year’s most talked-about cycling trends. These motors produce more than 1,000 watts of peak power and 110 Nm of torque. Category leader Avinox’s latest unit delivers an incredible 1,500 watts and 150 Nm of torque. Its power and performance have prompted Bosch and Specialized to respond with firmware updates that boost the torque and power of their premium drive units. Even so, the Avinox remains the most powerful drive unit available. But high-power motors aren’t without detractors, or potential consequences. Their use has sparked debate and hand-wringing in the mountain biking community over how much power is too much. Remember: “With great power comes great responsibility.”.

When you’re shopping for an electric mountain bike, you must factor in not only the motor’s power and features, but also the bike’s basic capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that since electronic mountain bikes are heavier than non-motorized bikes, you’ll want to consider a bike with more suspension travel than you have on your non-motorized bike. The longer your travel, the more cushion you’ll get when you encounter obstacles.

Most full suspension E-MTBs are in the 150- to 160mm travel range, which offers a nice balance of increased comfort and improved control for first-time buyers.

Sources indicate that there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding on trail systems.

According to recent reports, class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows people to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Other countries classify e-bikes differently, and many countries do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Most performance-oriented electric mountain bikes are Class 1. Electric mountain bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. A mid-drive motor will almost always offer more power. Because the extra weight on a mid-mount bike is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors. Mid-mount bikes do tend to be more expensive, but all of our favorite bikes feature this type of motor.

Battery Life, Range, Maintenance, and Safety.

In a recent development, on top of the motor, you’ll want to consider the battery size and range. More is always better for performance, but a battery with a longer range will also weigh more and cost more.

Sources indicate that as a bike's weight increases, it requires more effort from the rider to handle. This is especially an important consideration for smaller riders; extra weight can also become a bigger challenge at faster speeds, when you need to ride the bike more aggressively.

A lighter bike will offer better handling, but if you sacrifice too much battery capacity to cut weight, you may find yourself pedaling home with no assist if you take a wrong turn.

Like all e-bikes, E-MTBs can be pedaled as a normal bike if the battery dies, so you’ll still be able to get home, but it will require extra effort and possibly more time.

While we can confidently say a larger battery provides more range, it is difficult to accurately estimate any e-bike's exact range. Many factors impact an e-bike's range: How much boost you’re using (most power systems offer three or four settings), how much you weigh, the terrain you’re riding, how much climbing you’re doing, the air temperature, rolling resistance from the tires, and even how clean and lubricated the drivetrain is.

It has been revealed that don’t take any brand's word on its range claims. Start conservatively as you test your bike’s range. The more you ride, the better you’ll understand how far your batteries can carry you in different conditions. If your bike’s main battery isn’t cutting it, some models let you add an external range booster or swap the internal battery for a fresh one. Be warned: These accessories can be expensive!

Like all batteries, e-bike batteries do lose capacity every time they’re charged and discharged. Unfortunately, that means that the more you ride, the sooner you’ll need to replace your battery. Even so, an e-bike battery should give you years of reliable riding.

Follow your bike's manufacturer’s recommendations for storage, but most batteries will last longer if stored with about a 40-percent charge (but don’t forget to plug your bike in about six hours before riding, to make sure you start your ride with a full charge).

Batteries should also be stored at room temperature whenever possible and not left outside or in an unheated garage in freezing temperatures. Some bike brands, including Specialized, have a setting that will prevent the battery from charging fully. This feature is designed to extend the battery’s life, but you may want to disable the feature if the rides you regularly take use your battery’s full capacity.

If, after a few years, your battery loses enough capacity that you want to replace it, be sure to contact your bike’s manufacturer or local dealer and purchase a certified replacement battery through the brand or its dealer.

Recent findings suggest that don’t be tempted by cheaper options available online from third-party brands. These third-party batteries are generally not certified by bike brands and may void your bike’s warranty. More importantly, third-party replacement batteries often do not have vital safety features, and, as a result, these batteries have been identified as the cause of several serious fires.

There is presently legislation pending at the state and federal level that will bar the sale of non-certified batteries in the U.S., but they are still available as of this writing.

Sources indicate that while a handful of bicycle drivetrain manufacturers exist, almost every e-mountain bike will have either a Shimano or SRAM drivetrain. Both are reputable manufacturers that offer reliable shifting and a wide-ranging gear set. Some drivetrains feature electronic shifting. Such drivetrains offer quick and precise shifting, but they will add cost.

The added power of an e-bike puts more strain on a bike’s drivetrain. You can expect to replace your chain more frequently, but you can get more life out of your components if you back off the pedals when shifting, and ease the chain between gears instead of mashing the shifter and the pedal at the same time.

Industry observers note that given the increased weight of an electronic mountain bike, you’ll want to make sure yours is equipped with hydraulic disc brakes, as most are. These brakes offer lots of stopping power and modulation, which ensures you’ll remain in control regardless of your bike's weight, or how fast you go.

Recent findings suggest that several brands offer hydraulic disc brakes, though again, Shimano and SRAM usually lead the way. For additional power, look for bikes featuring four-piston brakes.

Bicycling has been reviewing bikes and gear for over 50 years, and our recommendations are grounded in decades of real-world experience. Our test team—Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy, Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips, Test Editor Dan Chabonov, and Senior Photographer Trevor Raab—collectively brings 75-plus years of ride-testing knowledge to every product we evaluate.

For this guide to electric mountain bikes, Matt and Tara led the charge, drawing from their deep category expertise and the team’s hands-on testing across a wide range of terrain and conditions. These picks reflect what we’ve learned through thousands of miles of testing: The E-MTBs that deliver the right mix of price, ride quality, trail capability, and pedal-assist performance. Whether you’re climbing faster, riding farther, or just having more fun, these are the best electric mountain bikes you can buy right now.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a blueprint, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Industry observers note that A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. #56717. Is Your AI Strength Plan Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In
