Tech Report: After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life.
  • If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”.
  • This newly introduced reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life. I scrolled past the phrase recently on social media: Somebody had designed it with colors and typography and posted it, apparently finding resonance in the sentiment.

I chuckled a little upon seeing it. If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”.

This newly introduced reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept. I’ve been running on and off for more than 50 years, some 85 percent of my life. I jogged along with my older brother when I was a girl, competed in high school as a teen, trained for a sub-3 marathon as a working professional in my 30s, plodded with a baby jogger in my 40s. Now, past 60, running has shape-shifted again. The transformation is different this time, the lessons deeper and, frankly, a little harder to grasp. But after a period of struggle, I’ve made peace with it. Because as usual, if you dare to listen, running will speak to you.

According to recent reports, most of us who run spend years or even decades seeking to improve, from a 5K to 10K, from breaking 4 hours in a marathon to then trying for 3:45. For a long time, wherever you are, improvement is possible, and change generally trends in one direction. Not every run, of course. The body has good days and challenging ones; that variability is a given, and progress is not a straight line. But we can expect a trajectory that provides a satisfactory feedback loop, one of betterment.

Industry observers note that inevitably, aging will bend the line of progression into an arc. We can know that and still have trouble seeing it at first, because the heavy legs or knee catching feels like just another hard day. Nothing a little rest or cross-training can’t solve.

It has been revealed that if seeing it is difficult, accepting it can be even harder. The forward march has been the natural state of things for so long. The battle waged for incremental increases in mileage or decreases in time was never easy. Shouldn’t I be pushing past this? Isn’t it what runners do?

Running taught me to be tough. For years, that served me even beyond the sport. In work, the tug of fatigue from long nights at the ad agency felt familiar and manageable as a long run. Giving birth called back the discipline of breathing through pain; the years of motherhood to come called in the lessons of patience, of quietly putting in the hours without immediate affirmation or result. I loved being a badass in the endurance sport of life. The ability to override tiredness felt powerful. I enjoyed telling myself I was fine when evidence pointed to the contrary. I relished pushing against edges and limits.

Recent findings suggest that until the day I woke, swung my feet over the side of the bed to stand, and felt the world spin wildly out of control. The floor rushed up to my face, and I curled in a ball seeking safety and stillness. Confusion mingled with nausea. I could feel the whirling even with eyes closed. The fetal position proved fitting. I’d spend years relearning how to be in this new world, where vertigo could strike at any time.

My first reaction was “I’ll fight!” Though for months that thought came while I was sprawled on the couch, unable to focus my eyes or lift my arms. A year of doctor visits, scans, and tests eventually ruled out physical problems and delivered a neurological diagnosis: vestibular migraine. As with other forms of migraine, the condition is underdiagnosed, women suffer more than men, and precious little is understood about what is actually happening in the brain to produce the symptoms. Some connection has been made to hormonal fluctuations, and, for some, a genetic link seems to exist; stress, I learned, is a reliable exacerbator of triggers.

My own onset remains a mystery.

Industry observers note that the impulse to fight landed ineffectually in space against the judo of forced rest. Any struggle against this opponent would only feed it. Somewhere along the way, a new understanding dawned: Vertigo was my body saying, “Stop.”.

Tough got me here, but it wasn’t going to get me through this next chapter. The fighting stance I’d adopted so long ago was not going to serve me well with the changes happening now. Some things about the body are not in our control, despite our best efforts. With precious few alternatives, I did something I never had before: I paused, I listened to what my body was saying, and I opened to the possibility of unlearning some things that running and life had drilled into me so very long ago. This time the lesson wasn’t about pushing through. It’s also not a sob story about slowing down. It is about acceptance.

In a recent development, now, three years since my first vertigo attack, something akin to gratitude has set in. The softening and adapting are treasured new tools. Essential new tools. Because the fact is: you don’t “overcome” aging.

Industry observers note that nowadays, when I’m feeling good enough to put on my shorts and running shoes, I might have an idea of what I’d like to do. But it’s just that, an idea. I start slowly, so as not to tweak a knee or an ankle. Eventually, my body will tell me what this day has in store. If I’m lightheaded and the sun feels too bright, triggering aural distortion, I walk and think, yes, it is a fine day for a walk. If I feel strong, I push to the degree I can and think, how wonderful, to feel good. Neither situation really surprises me anymore. None of it is bad. I feel lucky to be out here.

The point is this: It is all like this now. And if I can’t accept that in my running, I’m going to be in for an exhausting battle with every other part of aging. Don’t mistake this for giving up. I am working harder to stay fit than I have in a very long time. Pushing the pace all those years? It came pretty easy. It felt damned good. What I’m doing now takes more effort: Spin classes that give my knees a break... and where 80-year-olds are dusting me. Full-body lifting that leaves every hidden muscle protesting. Yoga classes that make it clear balance has never been a prerequisite for anything before in my life. The objective now isn’t performance—it’s simply to age as well as possible.

Industry observers note that there is no fairness in this, no way that this “should” go. Aging comes differently for us all, as an entire generation who grew up during the first running boom is now learning. Our running will change in its own way, a reflection of everything we have done before, plus the ineffable element of luck.

Industry observers note that my son-in-law’s mother is one of those seemingly defying the years. Pushing 60, she’s also pushing into fresh territory with a string of 50K trail races. Her streak of runs is proudly documented on Strava, which cheerily alerts me every time she becomes the “Local Legend” of some new stretch.

She’s excited, posting every day, a wide smile spread across her face. She exudes the joy of progress. I’m a bit envious, sure. I’m also glad for her. Both things can be true.

I have other friends who do not run anymore. In one way or another, their bodies—joints that didn’t respond to surgery, chronic illness that has sapped their energy—have let them know those days are done. The ones doing the best move on, find new challenges.

Recent findings suggest that my joy comes from somewhere else now. It’s not so much the running per se; rather, everything around it. The feeling of autumn’s first cool air on my shoulders. The smell of spring’s thawing mud. The sheer pleasure of moving through space outdoors one more day. In fact, these things are more present than before, without the distraction of pace and goals.

If my running taught me everything about how to persist, why wouldn’t it be the thing to teach me about how to let go? Our running is always “becoming.” Just as we are ourselves. We have an opportunity to learn from it, because the fact is that running isn’t the only thing that is changing.

As with everything else, it might not be the lesson you want, but it’s always the lesson you need.

It has been revealed that dagny Scott is the author of Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running. She is right now working on a book that explores the beauty in finding authenticity and acceptance in an aging body. Scott lives, writes, runs, and walks in Boulder, Colorado.

Breaking: Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we review the new EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap to see if it lives up to the hype of making cold and warm water training and racing more comfortable.
  • Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone.
  • In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we review the new EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap to see if it lives up to the hype of making cold and warm water training and racing more comfortable. (Photo: Courtesy EZ Gains).

Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an vital clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

According to recent reports, but first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

According to recent reports, EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The company notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

In a recent development, we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

Sources indicate that EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

In a recent development, you’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains claims the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

To evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

Recent findings suggest that the TLDR from my testing: Some new technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

First, EZ Gains states the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

It has been revealed that second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

Recent findings suggest that in my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Third, EZ Gains states the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

There are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I showed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

According to recent reports, which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

#56695. Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)

Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Getting faster isn’t just about training harder.
  • While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

Sources indicate that major picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

So how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

It has been revealed that recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, says run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as promptly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

Industry observers note that “As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in Fresh York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

It has been revealed that this logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” indicates Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

For example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

And remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, notes he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s important to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

Landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

If you’re relatively fresh to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

It has been revealed that fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

If you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s important to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

One of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form concerns getting worse as the run progresses.

In a recent development, the metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

If you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

For Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he states.

Recent findings suggest that if these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

In a recent development, and if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” states Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional strategy.”.

Industry News: Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future.
  • When I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future. It’s easy to use and reliable. It did exactly what I needed it to do—turn my bike into a trainer for offseason training.

When I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use. More than that, every shop team I’ve worked with would use the Wahoo Kickr Core as their trainer of choice. Then I was introduced to the Zwift Ride and realized I was not done buying trainers just yet.

As the shop’s service manager, I got firsthand experience assessing bikes after a season of sitting on the trainer; let alone season after season, year after year. The level of maintenance needed for those bikes was initially shocking to me as well as to the customer. Most of us are aware we need to do maintenance on our bikes that we ride outside, but it’s easy to forget about our unsung hero—our trainer bike sitting in the basement constantly covered in sweat, spilled drink mix, and getting the watts cranked into it day in and day out.

There’s a better way than just throwing your bike on the trainer for your offseason. The Zwift Ride V2 with the Wahoo Kickr Core is now my top recommended way to use a bike trainer. It’s easy to see why.

Sources indicate that for those who have multiple riders in one house, this may be one of the biggest benefits. When I had my bike set up on the Kickr Core it was harder for my wife to just hop on the trainer. Since my old trainer bike was carbon, even a simple saddle adjustment required a torque wrench. I’ve even gone so far as to change out stems to change the reach too—not the hardest thing to do, but by no means convenient. On the Zwift Ride, most fit adjustments are super easy and take just seconds.

The Zwift Ride 2 I’ve been on even has multiple crank length options set up in the cranks, so you just swap the pedals to a different hole in the crank to change the effective crank length. Taking out one more friction point between me and being able to start my trainer ride means I’m even more likely to get my winter trainer miles in.

In a recent development, the other day I was a few minutes into my warmup and I needed to adjust my reach a bit. I pulled the integrated 6mm Allen key out from its place under the top tube, easily adjusted the reach at the handlebars, tightened everything down, and reinstalled the tool all without interrupting my cadence. Having the tool I need to adjust just about anything on the bike is a fresh level of convenience I was not used to.

It has been revealed that as Matt Phillips pointed out in his Zwift Ride 2 review, “Mechanically, the Ride is almost primitive.” For clarity, this is by no means a negative—when it comes to a trainer bike, mechanically primitive but extremely functional is a best-case scenario. This bike has a chain that goes from the chainring, through a chain tensioner, around the Zwift Cog attached to the Wahoo Kickr, and back up to the chainring. There’s no derailleur, no front tire that needs air, no brakes to knock out of alignment. The handlebars don’t even turn, so there’s no headset to replace in the spring because it was sitting in a pool with sweat all winter.

In a recent development, on the other side, you’re saving your daily driver from a lot of unseen mechanical damage. As the snow thaws out on the roads, road riders are ready to get back in the saddle under the sun, but if you use your bike on the trainer all winter, it may need A LOT of love before it’s road-worthy.

A bike that sits on the trainer all winter collects significant corrosion in headset and bottom bracket bearings. The sweat that comes off your head drops straight onto your headset and sweat from your body (and any of those sticky drink mixes) drop straight down toward the bottom bracket. Then we get to the drivetrain. I’ve had bikes come in around March that need full drivetrain replacement: chainrings, cassette, and chain after a good season of indoor miles. Finally, we get to the handlebar—at a minimum you should replace that bar tape after a season riding on the trainer. This also gives you a chance to get the handlebar looked at to make sure all that corrosion (sweat) hasn’t eaten into the them.

It has been revealed that I’ve seen service tickets range anywhere from $100 to almost a thousand dollars just to get a bike off the trainer and ready to ride outside. For some people one season of trainer riding on the Zwift Ride 2 could be more cost-effective than using your road bike on a trainer.

Before an activity becomes a habit people are good at finding reasons not to do something. It doesn’t take long to setup a bike on the Wahoo Kickr Core, but even that little bit of set up time to pop your bike on the trainer is one more hurdle for you not to ride today. If you have to swap your cassette over from your bike to the trainer—you can almost forget about it.

In a recent development, it doesn’t just go for getting your bike on the trainer. This week in Pennsylvania we’re having a stretch of perfect riding weather—relatively low humidity, sunny, and temperatures between 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Next week’s forecast calls for colder temperatures and rain, also known as great indoor-riding weather. But this week, if I have a window of time to ride, I want to be able to just hop on my bike and go; I don’t want to have to take the bike off the trainer and reinstall my cassette before I can even start pedaling outside. With a dedicated trainer setup, I can just take my bike off the hook on the wall and roll away. Next week, when the weather goes south, I can just hop back on the trainer.

The Zwift Ride makes it easier to do things like use power-ups, steer the avatar, and toggle through screens, but those features are just an added bonus compared to the other reasons to pick one up. It is a burly, simple, near-flawless machine for riding on the trainer. It’s stable when putting out your max watts. The built-in tool makes it easy to accommodate different riders—including adjusting the reach. Even the bottle cages are designed to fit almost any bottle. The bike’s handlebar tray fits an iPad or other tablet well, but I pair it with a rolling trainer table if I’m using my laptop. You can buy the Zwift Ride itself, or as a package deal with Wahoo’s excellent Kickr Core 2, which gives you everything you need for a stress-free indoor riding season.

A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. #56693. Research Shows This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Research Shows This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time.
  • It has been revealed that but sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles.
  • So if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

It has been revealed that but sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

So if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

In a recent development, instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

It has been revealed that get the strength plan that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our upcoming progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

Sources indicate that to get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

Doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

What’s important to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

In a recent development, in the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

Six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

According to recent reports, the high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma notes his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

Sources indicate that first, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he says.

Plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”.

It has been revealed that doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma claims. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

If possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he claims. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”.

In this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

Scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.

#56692. Otso’s Waheela R Is a Gravel Race Bike Built Around Rider Choice

Otso’s Waheela R Is a Gravel Race Bike Built Around Rider Choice

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister tech giant, Wolf Tooth Components.
  • The Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission.
  • That longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister tech giant, Wolf Tooth Components. The Minnesota-based bike brand was founded in 2016 by the engineers behind Wolf Tooth, and the two companies share a home and a practical approach to bike design. Otso’s small lineup includes gravel, mountain, and fat bikes, offered with a level of custom options that puts most major brands to shame.

The Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission. Otso gave it a longer front end, a slacker head tube angle, aero-shaped tubing, and internal storage, all to build a bike that can be raced hard over rough terrain.

That longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding. The Waheela R felt composed at speed and gave me confidence on steep, loose descents. But it never felt like a handful when I slowed down for a tight turn. I also appreciated the choices Otso gives riders when setting up the bike, from cable routing to the parts that come on a complete build.

There are some compromises, particularly for riders who need one of the two smaller frame sizes. But after spending time on the Waheela R, I came away thinking that Otso got a lot of things right.

There’s nothing particularly flashy about many of the Waheela R’s frame details. It has a threaded BSA bottom bracket, a round 27.2 mm seatpost, an external seatpost collar, and a UDH derailleur hanger. In a world where it sometimes feels like every new bike comes with a proprietary part you’ll eventually have to track down, I find that extremely refreshing.

Perhaps the biggest example of Otso giving riders a choice is the cable routing. If you want a completely clean front end, you can route the lines through the handlebar, stem, and headset. If you’d rather keep them out of the headset entirely, there are ports at the head tube. Or you can do what I did and take the middle ground, running the lines under the stem and into the headset.

As far as I know, this is the only production bike that lets you choose between fully internal and external headset cable routing right out of the box. While brands might point to the small amount of extra weight added to the frame to accommodate this feature, I still think it can be worthwhile on more bikes, particularly ones aimed at regular riders rather than world tour pros.

The down-tube storage is another detail I like. Its opening sits above the bottle cage, so you can get into the compartment without removing your bottle. More importantly, the door isn’t also responsible for holding the weight of the cage and bottle in place. The compartment feels well sealed and has enough room for a flat kit and an emergency jacket.

It has been revealed that there are plenty of useful mounts, including space for three bottles, a top-tube bag, and a partial frame bag. Otso also includes fender mounts, though you won’t find cargo mounts on the fork legs. For a bike designed primarily around gravel racing, I think that’s a sensible decision.

Industry observers note that the frame is 1x-only and clears a round chainring up to 50 teeth. Rear tire clearance is 50 mm on medium through extra-large frames, but drops to 45 mm on the extra-small and small. That smaller-size limit of just 45 mm is the one frame detail that feels like a substantial miss for Otso.

Recent findings suggest that in general, while more tire clearance is good, I’m okay being in the minority of tech writers and saying that for most people 50 mm is plenty. At the same time, 45mm-frame clearance isn't enough in 2026, and I would probably advise riders considering the two smaller frame sizes to look at other options because of that one detail.

Sources indicate that the Waheela R has a longer front end and a slacker head tube angle than many gravel race bikes. A medium has a 405 mm reach and a 70.5-degree head angle. For comparison, a 54cm ENVE MOG has a 389 mm reach and a 71.25-degree head angle, while a 54cm Specialized Crux 5 has a 388 mm reach and a 71-degree head angle.

Industry observers note that the Otso also has a longer wheelbase: 1,058 mm on a medium, compared to 1,027 mm for the 54 cm MOG and 1,026 mm for the 54 cm Crux. The BMC URS is closer to the Otso’s approach, with a 410 mm reach, 69.5-degree head angle, and 1,070 mm wheelbase on a medium.

Industry observers note that one thing to keep in mind is that frame sizes don’t always line up between brands. The medium Waheela R is closer in stack and reach to a 56cm Crux 5 than to a 54 cm. Stem length, handlebar reach, and spacers all affect the final fit, so it’s worth looking closely at the geometry chart before ordering.

I spent a lot of time riding the Waheela R on all kinds of terrain, from smooth gravel roads and flowy singletrack to steep, loose doubletrack. If I could reasonably tackle something on a gravel bike, I rode the Otso on it. And just about everywhere I took it, the Waheela R was very enjoyable to ride.

The longer front end and shorter stem gave the bike a stable, confident feel, particularly when I was moving rapidly over rough ground. On steep, loose descents, I felt comfortable relaxing my grip on the bars and letting the front end roll and stabilize through rocks and ruts. The Waheela R never felt nervous or like it needed my constant attention to navigate every trail imperfection.

What impressed me was that the Waheela R didn’t feel sluggish when I slowed down. It was still easy to steer through tighter turns on singletrack, and I never found myself fighting the bike to get it pointed where I wanted to go. I probably wouldn’t choose it for a cyclocross race, but that’s also not what Otso designed it for.

Recent findings suggest that the bike was just as capable going uphill. On steep, loose climbs, I felt like the longer front end gave me room to move forward and keep the front wheel planted without giving up too much rear traction. It’s a subtle thing, but it helped me stay seated and keep moving when the grade got very steep.

The Waheela R also has the stiffness and responsive feel I expect from a gravel race bike. It felt eager to accelerate when I pushed on the pedals, and I never found the ride particularly harsh. That stated, I’d still rank the Specialized Crux 5 ahead of the Otso for comfort. The Waheela R strikes a good balance for a race bike, but it isn’t the smoothest gravel bike I’ve ridden.

Sources indicate that the Waheela R is very competitively priced, especially given how much freedom Otso gives you to customize the build. The frameset price is $2,950, but it’s the complete bike prices that really shine. A complete Waheela R with mechanical Shimano GRX 600 starts at $4,250. A SRAM Force XPLR AXS build starts at $5,450.

Of course, you can spend more if you want to. Otso offers upgrades including ENVE wheels and cockpit components, along with a range of Wolf Tooth parts and anodized colors. But what I appreciate most about the configurator is the ability to choose things like stem length, handlebar width, and seatpost offset when you order the bike.

According to recent reports, that can save you the expense and frustration of buying a complete bike, only to immediately replace parts to get the fit right. Depending on the build, you can also choose your wheels, tires, gearing, and cable routing. Some options add to the price, but you get to decide where you want to spend or save your money.

It has been revealed that it’s the kind of flexibility I wish more brands offered. Whether you want a relatively straightforward GRX build or a Force-equipped bike with ENVE wheels, Otso lets you put together the bike you actually want from the start.

It has been revealed that the Waheela R is a fun, capable gravel race bike, but what sets it apart for me is how much choice Otso gives riders. You can route the cables through the handlebar and headset, keep them entirely out of the headset, or choose something in between. Add in a threaded bottom bracket and a standard round seatpost, and you get a bike that will be easy to live with for years to come.

Sources indicate that that flexibility extends to the build options. Otso lets you choose your stem length, handlebar width, seatpost offset, wheels, and other parts when you order. The pricing is good, too. Even a Force AXS build decked out with ENVE wheels and components can come in under $10,000.

In a recent development, the biggest miss is tire clearance on the two smallest frame sizes. While medium through extra-large frames fit tires up to 50 mm, the extra-small and small are limited to 45 mm at the rear. For riders who want more tire volume for rough courses or the option to run wider rubber in the future, that will be a deal breaker.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Newly introduced York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1669 w)

What Nike Shoe Matches Your Running Style?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings.
  • Luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively.
  • It has been revealed that you can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Runners are a varied breed. Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings. Others may be training for an endurance event like a marathon or half marathon, with specific distance goals. You may be chasing a new PR, looking to hit the trails, or mixing running with other activities like lifting weights. So many different ways to run, so many shoes to choose from.

Luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively. Not sure which style fits your needs best? We’ve got you covered with the shopping guide below.

It has been revealed that you can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring. The Nike Pegasus line has offered that same dependability for more than four decades, and the technology just keeps getting better.

According to recent reports, the reason why the Pegasus Plus 2 works for daily, all-purpose running is its technology: Superlight ZoomX foam in the heel pairs with an exposed Air Zoom unit in the forefoot to deliver comfort and energy return that powers up every mile. Up top, a sleek mesh material offers both support and flexibility without letting your foot overheat, while a revamped forefoot shape gives your toes a little more wiggle room. And the classic Waffle outsole design has an updated diagonal pattern with flex grooves for better traction and ground feel, so you’re more in tune with your terrain. Plus, those textured laces are less likely to come untied—so you’ve got one less thing to worry about when you’re heading out the door.

Recent findings suggest that the Pegasus Plus 2 is also a good option to slip on for easy and slower recovery runs. Responsive and comfy without being super stacked, this shoe is the ultimate workhorse in your running closet.

In a recent development, for long runs and marathon training, you want max cushioning, like what’s found in Nike’s Vomero 18. Lightweight ZoomX foam stacked on top of responsive ReactX foam in the shoe’s midsole results in a plushy landing that has you feeling like you’re landing on a cloud with every step. Considering that the Vomero 18 is 13 percent more responsive than previous React technology (per the manufacturer’s own measurement), your legs feel less fatigued even as the miles add up.

An increased rocker design and pods placed strategically around the outsole allow for better push-off and smoother heel-to-toe transitions. The breathable engineered mesh material up top and plush padding in the tongue and lining help your feet stay cool and comfortable. This super cushy shoe that runs effortlessly is one of the reasons why RW shoe testers gush about it.

For those who like to customize their kicks, the shoe is part of the “Nike by You” line, allowing you to pick features like color and accents and even add your own text in the heel, tongue, and forefoot.

In a recent development, you’re not just a runner. You also rule the weight room, enjoy a good cardio class, and have been known to dabble in metabolic conditioning workouts. If you’re looking for an all-purpose training shoe, Nike’s versatile Free Metcon 7 fits whatever your workout ask. This sleekly designed cross-training shoe lets you have it all, from supporting multi-direction movements on the gym floor to dynamic cushioning when you want to hit the treadmill.

In a recent development, the shoe finds its multiuse purpose with a flexible design that features softer foam in the midsole and firmer foam in the heel for added stability. Plus, the full-length rubber outsole helps with traction on a variety of surfaces, including turf, concrete, and gym floors. You’ll also appreciate the webbed lacing and midfoot containment system designed to keep your foot firmly in place as you move around.

It has been revealed that for those who want a mixed-terrain shoe that can hit the road and trail and also handle inclement weather like rain and snow, the Vomero 18 Gore-Tex is a great choice. These waterproof shoes are designed to take on puddles, pebbles, rocks, and roots without missing a beat.

According to recent reports, the shoe has all the same stacked ZoomX and ReactX performance cushioning as the Vomero 18, plus a Gore-Tex waterproof liner to help your feet stay dry without getting too sweaty. The Storm-Tread outsole is specifically engineered for wet and slippery conditions, with an enhanced rubber compound for stronger grip and a thoughtful outsole pattern that keeps you grounded even on icy surfaces. Plus, the soft, protective mesh upper will keep your feet warm.

If you are looking for a shoe to race in, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is an update to Nike’s popular carbon-plated shoe. It’s even lighter than its predecessor, the Alphafly 3, (approximately 6.6 ounces compared to 7.1 ounces respectively) and offers more energy return to help you chase your next PR.

It has been revealed that that’s accomplished through its upgraded RF Air Zoom cushioning unit underfoot that uses vibration and frequency to create a smooth, comfortable ride, while the carbon fiber Flyplate gives you extra energy return to power through every mile. A slightly wider platform design compared to the Alphafly 3 also provides more stability so you can feel confident even on quick turns. And the wispy Atomknit 2.0 upper offers enough support to keep your foot firmly in place with as little added weight as possible.

Your shakeout run after a marathon or ultra should be about comfort at an easy pace. Think plenty of cushioning, a smooth, bouncy ride, and an unfussy upper. The Nike Vomero Premium ticks all those boxes, making it a good choice to slip on for post-marathon recovery runs.

Tired legs will appreciate a midsole that’s made up of ZoomX foam surrounding two energy-boosting Air Zoom units—one in the forefoot and one at the heel. The result is a light, comfortable ride with energy return that makes each step feel effortless and propels you easily along your route. You’ll want to wear this shoe for your daily runs for weeks after your 26.2-mile-and-beyond races.

Who doesn’t want to slip into something comfortable after a long run, or just a long day? The Nike ReactX Rejuven8 is just the thing, with a design that’s created to elicit all the aahs you can imagine. Thanks to React X technology in the upper and midsole, your feet will be surrounded in soft, responsive comfort. There’s extra room in the forefoot to allow your toes to rest and ventilation holes to allow your feet to breathe. Walking is easy and fluid because the sticky rubber outsole adds grip to the ground below you; therefore, no additional balancing act to get from one place to another. The result: A recovery shoe you’ll never want to take off.

In a recent development, we all love getting gifts, but shopping for shoes can be tricky when you’re not the one who will be wearing them. A little advanced knowledge can make a substantial difference in ensuring your present is truly appreciated. Here are some buying tips:.

Check what they already run in. If you can, look at the label inside a pair of running shoes they like, or ask someone who knows. Note the model, size, and width—running-shoe sizing may differ from their dress-shoe size—as well as any preferences, such as cushioning or toe-box room.

Check the return policy. See if the store has any specific limits on returns and exchanges, and if you can get a gift receipt so your giftee has the option to exchange the shoe for a different size.

According to recent reports, keep fit in mind. Remember that footwear largely depends on individual fit, with some shoes running bigger or smaller than the given size. When possible, avoid final sales (where the shoe is not eligible for returns) just in case there’s a fit concern.

Sources indicate that the Nike running shoes best suited for long runs and marathon training are the Nike Vomero 18. You want to make sure your shoe offers both stability and support to reduce injury risk and protect your joints. Many distance runners today prefer shoes with maximalist midsoles, which feature a large stack of foam to cushion against impact, as well as energy return rocker designs for faster push-off and landings. These are all things the Nike Vomero 18 delivers on.

When it comes to race-day itself, especially for half-marathons and full-marathons, many runners seeking a time goal prefer performance shoes like Nike’s Alphafly 4, which have a thin carbon plate for strong energy return and maximum speed.

Industry observers note that when looking for a recovery-run shoe, you want one that feels comfortable and provides plenty of support and a smooth, stable ride without being overly technical. The Nike Vomero Premium is the best Nike running shoe for easy recovery runs because it’s a shoe that delivers full-length cushioning and a roomy fit so your feet stay happy.

To choose the right size and width for Nike running shoes, go to a store that specializes in running shoes and try a few pairs on. Most running stores will let you jog around the floor (and some even let you jog around the block) so you have a sense of what works best. Running shoes should feel roomy but not so much that your feet move around a lot. You should be able to fit about a thumbnail’s width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. There also shouldn’t be any pressure on your pinky toe, and only a little bit of pressure on your significant toe.

Sources indicate that if you’re experiencing side pinching, bulging or spilling over, or flat arches, a wide shoe may be for you. These Nike models are available in wide widths: Downshifter 14, Pegasus 42, Revolution 8, Structure 26, Vomero Plus and Vomero 18.
