#56690. Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3047 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no shortage of fresh cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable.
  • In a recent development, our editors bring different perspectives to testing.
  • Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of fresh cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

In a recent development, our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

It has been revealed that I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

Sources indicate that that mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

According to recent reports, when I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates promptly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

Sources indicate that these aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

It has been revealed that A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

According to recent reports, despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

As a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

According to recent reports, its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them rapidly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

Sources indicate that spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

It has been revealed that I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

Recent findings suggest that the main issue I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

According to recent reports, now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

So far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

Debuted in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls quickly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In a recent development, in nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit issues. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

In a recent development, I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

Industry observers note that at $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

Industry observers note that the fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common problem I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

It’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

According to recent reports, I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

Recent findings suggest that the wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

Industry observers note that the sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

In a recent development, I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

Industry observers note that the Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full upgrade to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a major reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an enhancement to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

According to recent reports, but even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing revealed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 revealed to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

According to recent reports, other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In a recent development, in any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

Tech Report: 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • In a recent development, research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • In a recent development, the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

In a recent development, research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, indicates core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

In a recent development, the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

Industry observers note that to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Upcoming York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In a recent development, in addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun fresh ways, but also engage your brain.

Recent findings suggest that how to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

In a recent development, tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir notes. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

Industry observers note that how to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

In a recent development, why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

In a recent development, how to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir indicates. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir says.

Recent findings suggest that how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir says. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out. They can save your training, and I swear, they can be a ton of fun—really. Between the engaging, interactive streaming treadmill classes, and the ability to strip down to your skivvies and have no one see you sweat, it’s the perfect accompaniment to your marathon training, interval workouts, and even steady, zone 2 workouts. All from the comfort of your own home. And did you know that with many insurance prepares, you can pay for your treadmill with FSA dollars? That’s a solid fiscal choice, right there.

There are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been. They have more features, use less electricity, and are more versatile than ever before. Some are virtually personal trainers in and of themselves.

We’re in the process of testing a few new models, and we’ve just added the Urevo CyberMega, which is the first treadmill designed specifically for marathon training. It’s pretty freaking sick, I cannot lie.

Sources indicate that looking for a more heavy-duty treadmill that can handle higher speeds, longer miles, and more complex training aims? See our guide for the best advanced treadmills, which cost more but offer more training features and sturdier builds.

There’s really something special about this machine. The NordicTrack Commercial 1750 treadmill hits that “Goldilocks-level” sweet spot with its cushioning—it’s responsive enough to save your joints without making your run feel like a slog or an unstable adventure. And with a 60-inch belt, even our tallest testers with their gazelle-like strides had plenty of room to stretch out and feel steady.

Our testers absolutely gushed over the treadmill’s sleek, streamlined design, especially the Z-shaped console with its high-perched 16-inch screen. It’s perfectly positioned for runners who like to stay close to the controls. While we wished the cup holders were a bit deeper for our oversized water bottles, the slim arms offered a surprisingly stable grip, even when our hands got a little… enthusiastic.

It has been revealed that the 1750’s speed adjustments are pretty standard, going from 6 mph to a zippy 12 mph in 8 seconds. This is totally fine for 400- to 800-meter training, but for intense, quick-pickup speedwork, it’s not quite as snappy as some might like. Our testers did note one minor peeve: the lack of quick keys for 10 and 11 mph.

According to recent reports, we practically insist you dive into NordicTrack’s iFit program for an out-of-this-world experience. Our testers found its ability to read and adjust their runs to be nothing short of revolutionary during testing. While the high horsepower motor and Bluetooth speakers do make the machine a bit boisterous, it’s not at all distracting when you’re walking with your headphones on.

Despite its daunting price tag, the 1750 is a total workhorse that will supercharge your runs—and it goes on sale often. The built-in Netflix feature is a godsend, making miles absolutely fly by, and that cushioning is pure magic for your joints. Bottom line: the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 is a fantastic all-around package and a top-notch investment for most runners.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Review.

Sources indicate that the Horizon T101 treadmill proves you don’t need a huge budget for a fantastic workout. At a sale price of just $600, this compact folding machine impressed us with consistent performance over weeks of testing. It’s a low-to-the-ground, 20- by 55-inch deck, ideal for casual runners 6 feet and under.

The T101 boasts a three-zone running surface, offering extra cushioning where you land, less where you toe off, and a smooth transition in between for a supremely comfortable, low-impact ride. While it skips the fancy screens, its functionality shines. Connect to Strava or Peloton, or dive into workouts and courses via the free atZone app. Plus, there’s a perfect spot for your iPad to stream your favorite indicates!

The six built-in programs are straightforward, displaying calories burned, heart rate, distance, speed, and incline (up to 10 percent). While it can hit a 6-minute mile, be mindful: the speed and incline dials are sensitive—one haptic notch, not a full spin, increases your pace.

But you know what’s a real showstopper? The T101’s incredibly easy, one-step hydraulic fold. Just lift the back, and it zips up. To release, toe the center bar, and it gently lowers itself.

For its price, the T101’s features are unbeatable. It’s not for marathoners or speed demons, but for everyone else, it’s a solid win.

It has been revealed that horizon’s 7.0 folding treadmill is a robust upgrade, boasting a spacious 60-inch deck perfect for long strides, though its 20-inch width might feel snug if your mind wanders. Cushioning is excellent for long runs, but expect some bounce when the incline exceeds 5 percent—so perhaps skip the speedy hill work.

This machine is on the bulkier side, resembling a gym-quality unit, but its integrated features ensure easy setup. We loved the eye-level tablet holder, making streaming a breeze. Below, you’ll find a digital/manual console, fan, Bluetooth speakers, and two generously wide (if shallow) cup holders with room for your essentials.

Programming-wise, the 7.0 shines with its ability to link to Peloton, Apple Watch, and Samsung Galaxy watches, displaying calories and distance directly. Peloton classes synced smoothly, making transitions seamless.

In a recent development, A standout feature: knobs on the grips allow for effortless pace adjustments without breaking your stride. While there’s a subtle lag when decreasing speed, it’s barely noticeable at top speeds.

Recent findings suggest that at around $1,000 on sale, this treadmill offers impressive value. Its blend of convenience and comfort makes it a winner. Pro tip: opt for white-glove delivery—this beast is heavy, and assembly is a pain!

Full Horizon 7.0 AT Treadmill Review.

Industry observers note that marathon training demands months of relentless mileage, a crap ton of structured workouts, and more consistency than most of us think we’re capable of. The Urevo CyberMega is a treadmill that claims to be built specifically for the rigors of that beast of blocks. In a market crowded with all-purpose machines designed to serve everyone from casual walkers to occasional joggers to high-mileage baddies, the CyberMega is thinking of the needs of marathon runners first.

Recent findings suggest that that marathon-focused idea makes the entire experience. Rather than treating running as just one feature among many, the CyberMega is designed around the realities of high-volume training. According to the brand, every aspect of the machine is intended to support athletes preparing for long-distance races, making it a notably different proposition from traditional fitness-focused treadmills.

Industry observers note that there are marathon courses built into the app that control your ‘mill, there’s AI coaching to get you to your PR, and a fun competitive leaderboard where you are up against other customers. This treadmill is made to keep your training going when you can’t get outside and also? To keep it exciting. It is honestly fairly impressive and a ton of fun to run on.

I was also impressed by how smooth the run is and how compact the machine is. It folds easily, stores without much hassle, and feels dang streamlined for a treadmill made to support hardcore training. That’s also the biggest drawback. If you’re over 6 feet tall, this is not the ‘mill for you with a 52-inch-long deck. But in spite of the short deck, it landed on this list is because it’s a wide-open area that doesn’t feel impeded by the bars.

The rotary knob is another nifty feature. It’s simple, responsive, and super convenient during workouts, and has speed and incline adjustments feeling smoother and more intuitive than traditional button-based controls or rocker dials. Overall, if you’re gonna be a world major chaser, you might want to think about chasing them on this ‘mill.

According to recent reports, got a few runners in the family, or you’re a high-mileage runner? The NordicTrack 2450 is a seriously solid folding treadmill that’s got your back. It’s built tough, has great cushioning, and a huge 22-by-60-inch running surface, so you can just run without worrying about comfort and stability.

The Z-shaped handlebar and crossbar design are super minimalist, keeping the console right there when you need it, and giving you plenty of room to stretch out at the front of the belt.

You’ve got your standard speed and incline adjustments, and this baby can zoom from 6 to 14 mph in under 10 seconds—perfect for those quick interval bursts. It has those quick keys like the 1750, but sometimes it can be a little tricky to nail down specific speeds.

According to recent reports, where the NordicTrack really shines is its iFit programming. We’re talking thousands of workouts, even marathon courses! Yeah, it’s an extra cost, but seriously, it’s a huge motivator. And that big display? It’s awesome. You can pause your run to squeeze in some strength training or even stream your favorite demonstrates.

Fair warning, though: putting this thing together is a beast, so you might want to call in a pro. And while it’s not super loud, it might be a bit disruptive if you’re trying to sneak in an early morning workout while everyone else is still snoozing.

It has been revealed that the ProForm Carbon TLX is a robust and dependable treadmill, designed for those who appreciate solid performance over excessive features. Its simplicity allows for focused workouts, minimizing distractions so you can stay in tune with your run. While it offers connectivity for phones, tablets, and fitness apps like iFit, at its core, the Carbon TLX is a workhorse—a no-fuss machine ready for you to hop on, get your miles in, and hop off.

The treadmill features a responsive and cushioned surface that offers a pleasant bounce at higher speeds. Our testers found that despite the softer feel, the generous 60- by 20-inch deck allowed for a natural stride. However, I did occasionally feel myself drawing closer to the front console, so if you prefer more forward space, a different model might be better suited.

For speed enthusiasts, the Carbon TLX is a dream. It rapidly reaches its top speed of 12 mph, and manual buttons provide smooth transitions between speeds. The incline goes up to 12 percent, providing a challenging workout that feels surprisingly good, even uphill. A standout feature is the powerful fan, strategically placed to provide excellent airflow—a detail any woman who’s done the “lift the boobs to get air” maneuver will appreciate.

If you’re a first-time treadmill buyer or looking to stay within budget, the Carbon TLX offers exceptional value for its price.

The Bowflex T9 treadmill brings a punch of fun and functionality to home workouts, making it a standout pick for casual runners and fitness fans alike. The red center line on the belt isn’t just for show—it helps wandering runners stay in their lane, so every jog feels more confident (and a little less wobbly). The running surface is firm and comfortable, with just enough pep to keep things lively, while the compact, foldable design slides neatly out of the way after your workout adventure.

Sources indicate that the controls and incline? Well, they’re not winning any races. Adjustments take their time, so interval chasers might grumble about holding down those buttons like they’re cranking up a jack-in-the-box. But the T9 redeems itself with robust app compatibility—it syncs up with Peloton, Zwift, and even Apple Watch for gadget lovers, and has an oversized tablet holder for serious streaming or stats-watching mid-run.

Industry observers note that weighing in with a 350-pound weight capacity, a quiet motor, and speed toggles at your fingertips, this treadmill turns everyday training into smooth sailing. It may not be a speed demon, but the T9’s thoughtful features combine comfort and tech for an overall enjoyable ride.

The Echelon Stride 6 is the treadmill I’ve kept at home after running over 1,200 miles on dozens of machines testing them for this article. It’s a solid, foldable treadmill that fits well in small spaces without feeling cramped. The larger-than-expected deck is 20.5 by 60 inches, giving plenty of room for a natural stride, even at my height of 6 feet. The deck provides firm cushioning that’s comfortable but not overly soft, which I definitely prefer for a closer to road-like feel.

The fold-flat design is a major bonus. The mill is stupid easy to tuck away under a bed or stand upright in a closet or—how I do it—up against a wall behind a curtain. That noted, it’s heavy when folded upright, so moving it alone can be a pain. The treadmill has a powerful built-in fan and heart rate sensors, nice extras for longer sessions.

It has been revealed that overall, the Stride 6 isn’t flashy or cushioned like some high-end models, but it delivers a dependable run and great space-saving convenience. For a runner who values a firm deck, quiet motor, and compact footprint, it’s a practical choice that keeps me coming back.

Not everyone needs a treadmill for running, and we get that. Sometimes, what you need is access to movement and the ability to stay active all day long. Enter the Go Plus under-desk walking pad. It is the bridge between daily life and running.

I love using this walking pad when I am working. It’s calm and quiet, but allows me to keep my body and brain active when I'd otherwise be sedentary. It has a deck that is a wonderful size to fit under your standing desk, though I do think it could be just a teeny bit wider. It’s only about 50 pounds, and has wheels so you can maneuver it around your space easily. It’s remote-controlled for easy use, and best of all? You can store this gal vertically in your closet. (Just don’t forget about it in there!).

According to recent reports, each and every treadmill on this list has been thoroughly evaluated by our team of editors at Runner’s World. I have personally tested each and every ‘mill on this list. Additionally, we solicited input from other staff at our office, like News Editor Theo Kahler, who has a PR of 14:20 in the 5K.

According to recent reports, the team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly vital factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

Apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

Recent findings suggest that having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

Recent findings suggest that having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

The length of the deck is a trickier concern. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

If you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

Incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

Treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running prepares and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

It has been revealed that and perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

Motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

According to recent reports, speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

Sources indicate that we have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

It’s predictable. Greer states that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, upcoming to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

According to recent reports, it also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

There are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature reveals some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

When you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

You might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

In a recent development, you need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

It has been revealed that treadmills are a big piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most important safety factors before you purchase a latest treadmill for your home.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

#56686. 3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling.
  • As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.
  • Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling. Our regular eating schedules shift around social gatherings, holiday menus influence our usual food choices, and staying hydrated can take more effort without higher temperatures to drive our thirst.

As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.

Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.

Vitamin D deficiencies are common among athletes in winter, Maddie Alm, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Fueling Forward Sports Nutrition in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. That’s because shorter days and colder temperatures can mean less exposure to the sun’s UVB rays, which help our bodies produce vitamin D.

Sources indicate that alm explains that this vitamin not only supports strong bones, but also helps keep our immune and digestive systems functioning at their best. It plays an vital role in brain health and mood, too. According to the National Institutes of Health, low blood levels of the vitamin have been associated with a higher risk of depression.

The Fix: Get outside daily to catch some sunshine, and focus on eating more vitamin D–rich foods, with the goal to consume 600 international units (IU) per day.

According to recent reports, good sources of vitamin D include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, tuna, salmon, egg yolk, and mushrooms. Some cereals and orange juices are also vitamin D–fortified. For reference, three ounces of salmon contain 450 IU, one cup of cow’s milk contains 180 IU, one large egg yolk contains 40 IU, and one cup of fortified cereal contains 40 IU.

It’s a good idea, Alm adds, to check your levels through bloodwork once or twice a year and to consult a professional if your numbers come back low. If you have a hard time hitting your daily quota through food alone, you may benefit from taking a vitamin D supplement.

It has been revealed that runners can also overlook vitamin C intake this time of year, states Sakiko Minagawa, RD, a registered dietitian for the Division of Sports Medicine at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio and two-time Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, supports immune health, which is especially important during cold and flu season.

In a recent development, our bodies also need vitamin C to produce collagen, a protein that’s essential for tissue growth and repair. “While vitamin C may not prevent you from outright getting sick, some research shows that it may decrease the duration of cold symptoms,” Minagawa explains.

In a recent development, the Fix: Up your consumption of foods with vitamin C, such as bell peppers, citrus fruits, greens, and strawberries. Women should aim for 75 milligrams per day, while men should aim for 90 milligrams daily.

You’ll get about 210 milligrams from one large red or orange bell pepper, and 90 milligrams in a cup of raw strawberry halves—each of which achieves your recommended daily dose.

Because vitamin C helps with iron absorption, Minagawa suggests pairing the two whenever possible. Some meals she recommends are a spinach salad with strawberries, an omelet with spinach and red bell peppers, and tomato soup with lentils or black beans.

Industry observers note that in the winter, you might not end your run with a dry mouth and sweat-soaked shirt like in the summer, but it’s still critical to hydrate. “Even when it’s cold, you still sweat,” states Minagawa, which means you still need to replenish fluids throughout the day, as well as before and after a workout.

Similarly, your midrun fueling and hydrating remain just as crucial for performance. It’s true: Tearing open an energy gel with gloved hands can pose a real challenge. But, if you’re doing long runs through the colder months, you still need to consume enough carbohydrates during your effort.

In a recent development, the Fix: Minagawa suggests carrying a water bottle that you can easily drink from and refill throughout the day. If you have a hard time sipping on plain water, remember that soups, broths, and hot chocolate can also help you stay hydrated—and can double as recovery fuel.

Don’t forget about fresh fruits and vegetables, either, as they can help with hydration. Some great in-season options that can contribute to your overall fluid intake include grapefruit, clementines, pomegranate, kiwi, squash, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, pears, kale, and cabbage.

During your winter long runs, experiment with fueling options other than energy gels and chews. Some great alternatives you can easily carry in a small plastic baggie include salted Medjool dates, boiled red potatoes, dried fruit, pretzels, and even candy.

Recent findings suggest that bad weather conditions, scant daylight hours, and more limited racing opportunities make winter a time for many athletes to dial back their training. Taking an off-season can benefit you in the long haul, but Minagawa encourages runners to still stay active—even if that means swapping some runs for walks, bike rides, easy swims, or elliptical sessions.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t want to depart from those year-round healthy habits, Brianna Butler, RD, a registered dietitian, co-owner of Stef & Bri Wellness in Texas, and former professional WNBA athlete, previously told Runner’s World. The same applies to your nutrition.

In a recent development, “The biggest mistake runners make is that, when it’s the off-season, they’re off everything—they say, ‘I’m not doing anything, I’m going to eat whatever’—they’re just winging it,” Butler says. “It shouldn’t be all or nothing. We want to make sure we’re nourishing our bodies well year-round.”.

If your training load changes significantly, pay closer attention to your hunger cues to make sure your nutrition matches your energy needs.

The Fix: Maintain a daily exercise routine you enjoy, prioritize nutrient-dense meals and snacks, and resist making drastic changes to your diet.

If you do find yourself feeling sluggish this time of year, it can be tempting to repent with cleanses, detoxes, and extreme exercise regimens. But such quick fixes rarely pay off in the long run, Alm warns, as they put you at risk for injury, burnout, and subpar seasons to come.

Recent findings suggest that alm claims not to stress if you ditched your typical eating and training schedule for a few weeks and are feeling less energetic as a result. When you return to your usual healthy habits, your body will naturally find its sweet spot. “Trust the process and don’t panic,” Alm advises, because our bodies may change as we move through different training phases. “It is okay to not be at your leanest year-round.”.

Recent findings suggest that the smartest path forward? Do your best to move your body daily, fuel it with what it needs, and give yourself permission to rest when you’re tired. That way, you’ll find yourself feeling strong and ready to train hard again come spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training plan for the offseason.

For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

Recent findings suggest that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training initiative.

In a recent development, so many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

It has been revealed that today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch quickly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

Sources indicate that one of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

Sources indicate that recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Plan accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Recent findings suggest that your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your plan week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout initiative. It’s notable to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I type this, I’m jumping through the various hoops involved in buying a 2023 Tesla Model Y, a rather expensive, luxury “crossover” that is absolutely loaded to the gills with excess: all wheel drive, faster acceleration than a Lamborghini, enough space for seven people and enough computer gadgetry to function as a small Google data center.

Enhancement: Looking for the ongoing tracker page? It’s here at “The Model Y Experiment“.

The total net cost of this thing to me after all the taxes and tax credits* will be about $52,000, which is just a stunning amount higher than the Honda van it is replacing. That old classic cost me $4500 when I bought it off of Craigslist twelve years ago, and it had served me dutifully until just last month, crisscrossing the mountains and deserts of this country and also helping to rebuild a considerable swath of houses in my neighborhood.

Sources indicate that I’m supposed to be a frugality-oriented financial blogger, and I’m also known for hating car culture – I think most people use cars about ten times more often than they need to, and most people drive cars they can’t afford. So why the hell am I buying a new one?

It has been revealed that from those first three paragraphs, you can see I’m feeling plenty of self-mockery and ridicule over this fresh purchase. If you’re also a naturally frugal person, you can surely relate to the thoughts and you probably also agree with me that I’m off my rocker.

Recent findings suggest that and indeed, I’m still on-board with frugality and healthy self mockery. After all, it was this overall life philosophy that earned me an early retirement 18 years ago, which provides all of the glorious freedom I enjoy now.

It was also the philosophy that allowed me to procrastinate on buying this expensive car for the last four years, even as countless people both close to me and out on the Internet egged me on and told me I should just loosen up and treat myself.

But there’s a classic slogan that applies to many areas of life, and it is something I like to dig up and ponder every now and then:.

Won’t get you where you’re going.”.

How does that piece of wisdom apply to frugal living and enjoying a long life of early retirement?

A quick story from a recent run to the grocery store will explain:.

I was standing there in the bakery aisle, hoping to restock with a loaf of Dave’s Killer Bread for the next day’s breakfast with some visiting friends. But since this was in a standard grocery store rather than the Costco where I usually shop, the damned stuff was priced at an eye-watering $6.99 per loaf (instead the $4.50 or so I’m accustomed to paying, and even at the bulk store this stuff is about double the price of normal bread).

“WHO THE HELL DO YOU THINK YOU ARE, TRYING TO SELL BREAD FOR SEVEN BUCKS!!!”.

Then I went through a whole mental battle of what I call Grocery Shopping With Your Middle Finger:.

“Should I just boycott this bullshit?”.

“Hmm I wonder if any of the other competing brands are any good?”.

“What else is a good substitute for bread for this breakfast?”.

And then thankfully, after exhausting all other mental options, I settled on the correct one:.

“JUST BUY THE BREAD YOU DUMBASS!”.

“Because you are never going to wake up in the future and look at your bank account and think, shit, if only I had an extra $2.49 in there I would be a happier person.”.

That night, I came home from the store and shared this funny tale with one of my guests. He understood perfectly because he too had earned his own retirement through a lifetime of grinding in tough jobs and disciplined frugality. And despite the fact that he has a net worth several times higher than mine, he admitted that he faces exactly the same mental battles over splurging on himself.

This same friend gives freely to charitable causes, has supported a local school for decades, and is always the first one to pull out the checkbook if a friend has hit hard times or is looking for a trusted business investor.

But he still has trouble bringing himself to take an Uber to the airport instead of riding the bus which takes an hour longer.

We both realized that we were being too cheap with ourselves, and we needed to work on it. And we came up with a set of three ideas that should hopefully work together to help us have more fun with our life savings, while we are still alive:.

Principle #1: The Minimum Spending Budget:.

It has been revealed that suppose you’ve done well over the years and amassed a pile of productive investments worth about two million dollars. Yes, this is a lot of money for most people, and that is the point: this hypothetical person truly has it made.

It has been revealed that but as it turns out, most Mustachians I know with this level of wealth are still living very efficient lives, usually with a spending level of under $40,000 per year. On top of that, they typically live in a mortgage-free house and still have various forms of side income from a small business or two.

The 4% rule tells us that this person should be fairly safe spending up to about $80,000 per year from that cozy nest egg, even if they never earn any other money.

In a recent development, if this person wanted to be ridiculously conservative and set the spending rate at 3%, that still leaves about $60,000 of fun money every single year.. Plus, again, any side income, future inheritances, and social security income only add to the surplus.

Thus, a reasonable minimum spending level for this person might be $60,000 per year.

And in most cases, they know this, but still go right on living on $40k or less and claim they have everything they could ever want.

But if you watch carefully you’ll still catch them firing up the middle finger at things like $6.99 Dave’s bread or the $14.00 Cabernet at the restaurant or driving around in a gas guzzler even when they would prefer to have a proper, modern electric car.

Sources indicate that and whenever these people do get extra money, their first instinct is to stash it away on top of the already-too-big pile. In diagram form, their money flow looks like this:.

Note that while this person is great at accumulating money through that major red arrow firing money back into the ‘stash, their “fun stuff” arrow appears quite flaccid and withered.

Principle #2 – the Dedicated Money Wasting Account.

Lifelong habits are hard to break, and it’s sometimes hard to “waste” your own hard-earned money on things that seem frivolous, even when you know intellectually that you have way more money than you’ll ever spend.

But have you ever noticed that if you are spending somebody else’s money, preferably an anonymous corporation, it feels different?

For example, when you’re on a business trip and you just show up at the dining table to eat and drink and you never see the bill, you probably don’t fret about the prices, right?

The key is to make your own money feel like somebody else’s, and you can do it like this:.

Principle #3 – The Splurge Accountability Buddy.

Many of us frugal people tend to stick together. And most of us have different versions of the same problem: we know logically that money is plentiful these days, but our emotions keep us stuck in our old ways of optimizing too much.

But I find that when I team up with local friends who are actually trying to battle these same habits, we can question each other’s decisions, call out cheapness when we see it, and cheer on splurges when we know the other guy would enjoy it.

My super wealthy friend from above has become much better about treating himself (and his family) to quality goods for the home, amazing trips together, and just a general reduction in his stress over being “efficient with money”.

My friend and HQ co-owner Carl (Mr. 1500 Days) has finally replaced his beaten-down minivan with a spiffy new Chevrolet Bolt electric car, and is loving that leap into the future.

It has been revealed that and of course Mr. Money Mustache, after squeezing one final mountain road trip out of his 23-year-old Honda van, is finally allowing himself to get the Tesla he has been talking about for half a decade.

A recent life change (becoming a co-owner of a fixer-upper vacation rental compound in beautiful Salida Colorado) has reignited the travel fire in my heart and made me realize how much I do love getting out to distant places for visiting, mountain biking, gathering with groups of friends and my favorite activity of all: Carpentourism.

Running the Numbers: how ridiculously expensive is this car?

In a recent development, this is the perfect start to my experiment in spending more. Realistically, a $50,000 car is going to cost me about $10,000 more per year than my old van was burning. With the biggest costs being these:.

Sources indicate that since I personally had a spending deficit of several times more than $10k per year, I figure this is a solid first step. And, since the car’s primary purpose is things like epic camping trips, dream dates, and  long adventures around the country, it will definitely help me spend more on experiences, hotels, and go out to dinner a bit more often as well.

“This Privileged Rich Folk Talk is Making Me Sick, why don’t you give your money away to charity, or to me?”.

In general, I agree: the world has problems and the richer you are, the more you should consider giving generously.

But also, to be honest, the whiny people who constantly send complaints like this out to strangers on the Internet really need to get a life. It’s great to encourage philanthropy through positive examples, but completely unproductive to send negativity to shame people you don’t even know for not following your own personal value system. The world has seen more than enough of this.

According to recent reports, on top of that, this one-sided thinking can be counterproductive. Both of my friends have given generously throughout their lifetimes. In my own case, I have donated over $500,000 to the best causes I could find during the years I’ve been writing this blog, but I was still refusing to let myself replace that 23-year-old van.

And that overthinking was leading to even more of a scarcity mentality, as I compared my own meager spending to these bigger numbers of my donations, and found myself thinking things like,.

Industry observers note that “Damn, I’m spending $100 on this dinner date which sounds like a lot, but I also spent ONE THOUSAND TIMES more on donations last year, which sounds like even more. Maybe I am spending too much and need to cut back on EVERYTHING!”And then the fear side of my brain would illogically chime in: “Yeah and you’re going to make us run out of money and be poor forever! waaaah waaaah! Cut back and optimize and conserve!”.

I think there is a happy medium here.

Yes – be a super, duper responsible steward of your life savings.

And yes, give generously with all your heart to charity.

It has been revealed that but yes, it’s also okay to set aside a portion of the money you’ve earned, for frivolous spending on yourself and those closest to you. You’re not a bad person for having a few nice things.

It’s okay to pay that extra hundred bucks to sit a bit closer to the front of the airplane instead of the back if it helps you enjoy your vacation and spend a joyful half hour walking FREE at your destination while the 49 rows of people behind you fuss infuriatingly with their shit in the overhead bins.

It’s okay to buy the frozen berries at Whole Foods even though they cost eight times more than Costco charges, if it spares you from making a second unpleasant trip through parking lot hell.

And as for me, I am calling it okay to, at last, double flip the Autopilot stalk in my upcoming Tesla and lean back as it it shoots me gracefully through even the highest mountain passes, forever leaving the desperately underpowered wheezing and gear shifting and noise* of the gasoline era behind, forever.

Rest in Peace, Vanna – 1999-2023.

* How to get rid of an old vehicle:.

I ended up using an online car salvage service called Peddle*, at the recommendation of a friend. With about five minutes of entering the details of my old Honda, their system offered me $715, and then a towtruck came and took it the next day – and actually gave me the payment in cash, which I found kind of fun. I made a point of using all of that money for splurges like dinners out, in keeping with the theme of this article.

* I later signed this blog up for Peddle’s affiliate program so that link will benefit MMM if you use it.

Recent findings suggest that * A useful tip for more effective splurging:Try to find the truly negative aspects of your life and focus any additional spending on improving those things. But it’s a subtle art so you have to get it right if you want lasting results in happiness.

You don’t want to just reduce hardship or challenge like hiring someone to take care of every aspect of your house, because overcoming daily hardships and having significant accomplishments provides the very core of our life satisfaction.

You also don’t want to just upgrade the things that are already good in your life. For example, a friend of mine is a gourmet coffee expert, and he suggested that I upgrade my setup at home to include on-the-spot roasting, and fancy grinding and brewing equipment. But I already love the good quality coffee I buy off the shelf from Costco, so it would be counterproductive to invest time or money into changing this part of my life.

But when you have something that causes you regular angst and stress, whether it’s a leaky roof that makes you dread rain, or a long commute that makes you dread the daily traffic jam, or a body that is giving you trouble due to not being in the best of shape – those types of things are probably a good target for improvement.

In the case of my car situation, I had a Nissan Leaf which is wonderful to drive, but doesn’t have the range to travel anywhere outside of the Denver metro area. Then I had the van which is a clunky beast to drive, but is otherwise an amazing road tripper because I could bring along whatever and whoever I wanted. But the van was getting increasingly unreliable in several hard-to-fix ways which was making me nervous every time I thought about long distance travel. Which was causing me to avoid certain trips and miss positive lifetime experiences.

In other words, my lack of a reliable long-range car was a small but consistent source of negative stress.

Sources indicate that finally, Vanna gave me the gift of a final hot and smelly transmission failure on a mountain pass on the way home from my latest project in Salida. It was just the nudge that I needed. And now I already feel excitement rather than dread at the prospect of all the road trips in the coming decades!
